title: Financial literacy in the digital age—A research agenda
authors: Koskelainen, T.; Kalmi, P.; Scornavacca, E.; Vartiainen, T.
tldr: Digitalization transforms financial services and consumer behavior, necessitating an updated conceptualization of financial literacy that integrates digital literacy components.
problem_and_motivation: Traditional financial literacy frameworks developed for an analog world may be inadequate in the current digital financial landscape. Despite the pervasiveness of digital financial services and technologies, little is known about how digitalization specifically influences individuals' financial literacy and financial capability.
approach: Conducted an integrative literature review using databases including ProQuest, EBSCO, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar.
Applied a two-stage selection process, screening 603 papers to identify 29 peer-reviewed studies relevant to digital financial literacy.
Focused on papers at the intersection of finance and digital technologies, excluding those focused solely on financial education or general digitalization.
Adopted a concept-centric review framework to organize and synthesize findings.
Classified selected papers into four core disciplines: finance, economics, finance and economics, and information systems.
Used the search string ('financial behavior' OR 'money management' OR 'personal finance') AND (digital OR 'digital literacy' OR digitalization) AND 'financial literacy'.
findings: num: 80% of millennial smartphone owners use their device for transactional financial purposes, and 90% for informational purposes.
Identified three main themes in the intersection of finance and digitalization: Fintech, Financial behavior in digital environments, and Behavioral interventions.
The literature comprises 17 papers in finance, 6 in economics, 2 in finance and economics, and 4 in information systems.
Digital financial literacy measurement has focused heavily on behaviors, which may be problematic due to consumer heterogeneity.
Fintech presents both opportunities (enhanced access, tailored products) and risks (misuse, fraud, data confidentiality, digital profiling).
Loss of cash payments and pervasive digital financial services make consumers less aware of their spending.
Smartphone app use increases salience of credit card transactions and results in reduced spending.
Nudging and digital nudging are increasingly used to influence consumer financial behavior, with ethical concerns about transparency and freedom of choice.
Existing digital financial literacy assessment items include conducting online shopping, using online/mobile banking, and initiating digital financial transactions.
Four key areas for future research identified: updating financial literacy curriculum, developing digital teaching tools, measuring digital financial literacy, and public-private collaboration.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a comprehensive integrative review that synthesizes prior literature on financial literacy within the context of digital transformation. It identifies three major thematic areas—Fintech, financial behavior in digital environments, and behavioral interventions—that collectively shape the emerging domain of digital financial literacy. The paper proposes a conceptual framework for digital financial literacy and financial capability and outlines a research agenda with four key priorities. It highlights the insufficiency of traditional financial literacy measures in the digital age and calls for the integration of digital literacy components. The paper also underscores the need for public-private collaboration to create more inclusive financial landscapes.

topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: The paper was systematically scanned against all topic domains in the taxonomy. The topics most directly covered include data privacy and security (10.A), as the paper extensively discusses digital profiling, fraud, and information security risks. Financial behavior themes (1.C, 5.A) were flagged as medium relevance since the paper reviews how digital environments affect consumer behavior and spending. Budgeting strategies (7.A) and mobile design (9.A) were also medium relevance due to discussions of spending awareness and app usability. User trust (10.B) was medium relevance based on perceived insecurity concerns. Topics related to culturally specific practices (2.A), expense categorization (3.A), and classification approaches (5.C) were considered low or contextual because the paper does not address these in detail. Other domains such as predictive modeling (6.A, 6.B), anomaly detection (8.A, 8.B), and evaluation frameworks (12.A, 12.B) were rejected as the paper does not discuss algorithmic or computational methods. The overall topical coverage centers on the conceptual and behavioral implications of digitalization for financial literacy rather than system design or algorithmic implementation.
